Oncological Conditions

Oncological conditions — cancer types, cancer treatments, chemotherapy side effects, palliative oncology care.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe common cancer types and staging
  • Explain chemotherapy side effects and management
  • Explain nursing care for oncology patients

In simple terms

Oncological conditions (cancer) are diseases where abnormal cells grow uncontrollably and can invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body. Nurses play a key role in cancer care — from symptom management to chemotherapy administration and end-of-life support.

Common cancers

Cancer Risk factors Key signs
Breast cancer Female gender, family history, age, HRT Breast lump, nipple discharge, skin changes
Lung cancer Smoking, asbestos, radon Cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain
Colorectal cancer Age, family history, diet Change in bowel habit, blood in stool, weight loss
Prostate cancer Age, family history, race Urinary symptoms, elevated PSA
Lung cancer Smoking, asbestos, radon Cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain
Leukaemia Bone marrow cancer Fatigue, bleeding, infection, bruising

Nursing care

  • Chemotherapy — administer safely (PPE), monitor for side effects (nausea, vomiting, myelosuppression, alopecia), manage side effects
  • Pain management — assess pain regularly, administer analgesics as ordered, use non-drug methods
  • Infection prevention — hand hygiene, avoid crowds, monitor for fever (neutropenia = emergency)
  • Nutrition — encourage high protein, high calorie diet; manage nausea and poor appetite
  • Patient education — teach about treatment, side effects, when to seek help, self-care

🔴 Febrile neutropenia = emergency

Fever (>38°C) in a chemotherapy patient is a medical emergency — may indicate neutropenic sepsis; report immediately, start antibiotics as ordered.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Chemotherapy administration — administer safely (PPE, double gloves), monitor for infusion reactions, manage side effects
  • Infection prevention — hand hygiene, avoid crowds, monitor temperature (fever = emergency in neutropenic patients)
  • Pain management — assess pain regularly, administer analgesics as ordered, use non-drug methods
  • Nutrition — encourage high protein, high calorie diet; manage nausea and poor appetite
  • Patient education — teach about treatment, side effects, infection prevention, when to seek help

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Common cancers: breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, leukaemia.
  2. Chemotherapy side effects: nausea, vomiting, myelosuppression, alopecia, mucositis.
  3. Febrile neutropenia = fever (>38°C) in a chemotherapy patient = medical emergency.
  4. Chemotherapy safety: PPE (gloves, gown, mask, goggles); double gloves; cytotoxic waste disposal.
  5. Patient education: infection prevention, medication adherence, when to seek help.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. TNM staging: Tumour size, Node involvement, Metastasis.
  2. Chemotherapy cycles: treatment given in cycles with rest periods between.
  3. Hair loss (alopecia) is usually temporary; hair regrows after treatment ends.
  4. Peripheral neuropathy: numbness/tingling in hands and feet (certain chemotherapy drugs).
  5. Tumour lysis syndrome: rapid cell death causing electrolyte imbalances, kidney injury.

📌 Memory trick

Chemotherapy side effects: NAUSEA — Nausea, Alopecia, Ulcers (mucositis), Neutropenia, Ulcers (mucositis), Anaemia.

60-second revision

  • Oncological disorders: cancer types (breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, leukaemia).
  • Chemotherapy side effects: nausea, vomiting, myelosuppression, alopecia.
  • Febrile neutropenia = fever >38°C in chemotherapy patient = emergency.
  • Chemotherapy safety: PPE, double gloves, cytotoxic waste disposal.
  • Patient education: treatment, side effects, infection prevention, when to seek help.

Test yourself

Febrile neutropenia is:

Answer: A. Febrile neutropenia = fever (>38°C) in a patient with neutropenia (low neutrophils) — medical emergency.

Chemotherapy extravasation means:

Answer: B. Extravasation = vesicant drug leaking into surrounding tissue — causes tissue necrosis; stop infusion, aspirate, notify doctor.

PPE for chemotherapy administration includes:

Answer: B. Chemotherapy requires PPE (gloves, gown, mask, goggles) to avoid skin contact and absorption.

TNM staging in cancer:

Answer: A. TNM staging: Tumour size and extent, Node involvement, Metastasis (spread to distant sites).

Hair loss (alopecia) from chemotherapy:

Answer: B. Chemotherapy-induced hair loss is usually temporary; hair typically regrows after treatment ends.
